title.text: National Museum of the Philippines - Butuan

title_en.text: National Museum of the Philippines - Butuan

tagline.text: A museum of the thousand-year-old Butuan balangay boats and golden relics

location.label: Location
location.text: Bayanihan district (near City Hall), Butuan City, Agusan del Norte

children.text: The National Museum of the Philippines - Butuan is a regional branch of the national museum. It displays balangay (Butuan boat) parts excavated in Butuan, pottery, gold ornaments, wooden coffins and other archaeological finds, along with everyday tools of the indigenous peoples of the Caraga region. It is a fitting starting point for exploring Butuan's history.

The National Museum of the Philippines - Butuan is a regional branch that the National Museum of the Philippines operates in Butuan City, Agusan del Norte. Wikipedia's list of National Museum satellite museums includes it as the Caraga regional museum and states that it opened in 1978. Butuan is a special city for Philippine archaeology. Researchers describe the area where the Agusan and Masao rivers meet as a center of trade and gold working from around the 10th century, and this museum gathers the evidence.

The museum is known to have two main galleries. The Archaeological Hall holds objects that came out of the ground, such as stone and metal tools, woodwork, pottery, goldsmithing and burial coffins. The Ethnological Hall displays objects used in everyday life today by the people of Butuan and the indigenous groups of the Caraga region. Travel bloggers report items from groups such as the Higaonon, Tiruray, Mamanua and Bukidnon, boats and fishing tools from the Agusan Marsh, equipment for making laksoy (palm wine) and farming tools. Displays are sometimes rearranged, so check before you visit.

What made this museum famous is the Butuan boats. In the 1970s, residents searching for alluvial gold near the Masao River found the remains of ancient plank-built wooden boats, and excavation of Boat 1 began in 1976. Locally the boats are called balangay or balanghai. They were built with a traditional Austronesian method: plank edges are joined with wooden pegs and lashed with fiber cord to rib-like internal frames, and there is no true keel. According to the Wikipedia summary, accelerator mass spectrometry dating placed several boats mostly between the 7th and 10th centuries, and Boat 1 was reported at 777–988 CE. Both the museum literature and Wikipedia state that the boats were declared a national cultural treasure by Presidential Proclamation No. 86 on March 9, 1987.

For visitors this is not a large museum. Even so, it makes a good first stop in Butuan, because you can see in real objects how southern Mindanao traded with China and Southeast Asia a thousand years ago. The city as a whole is covered in the Butuan entry, so read this one with a focus on the museum itself and its link to the balangay sites. Opening hours and admission rules differ between sources, so it is safest to check the National Museum's announcements or confirm locally just before you go.

This is the museum's centerpiece. Travel bloggers report that wing-shaped parts, planks, rib-like frames and a scale model are on display. Wikipedia states that Boat 1 is exhibited at this museum and that part of Boat 5 is also here, though most of it is in storage. Which parts you can see may change over time.

blocks.title: Pottery and Chinese trade ceramics in the Archaeological Hall

children.text: Jars and ceramics show that Butuan traded early with China and many other parts of Asia. The appeal lies less in showy beauty than in reading how the pieces were found and what they mean. Take your time with the captions.

blocks.title: Gold ornaments and traces of gold working

children.text: Butuan is known as an old center of goldsmithing. Wikipedia's article on the Butuan Ivory Seal says that more than a hundred clay crucibles and gold-processing tools were found at one village site. The museum is described as showing gold ornaments and other goldwork. The Golden Tara of Agusan is said to be at the Field Museum in Chicago, so assume you will not see it here.

The ivory seal, dated to around the 10th century, and the silver strip of the 14th–15th centuries are famous for their undeciphered writing. However, the ivory seal is said to be kept at the National Museum in Manila, so check locally whether the original is on display here.

Displays show wooden coffins and burial customs. One visitor account reports that a curator explained that skulls deliberately shaped in infancy signified aristocracy. View them quietly and listen to the explanations.

blocks.title: Everyday tools of Caraga indigenous peoples

children.text: Clothing and tools of the Higaonon, Tiruray, Mamanua and Bukidnon, boats and fishing tools from the Agusan Marsh, and laksoy distilling equipment are introduced. You can see at a glance living skills that are hard to find at village markets or outside museums.

After seeing the parts at the museum, continuing to the Balangay Shrine in Libertad, the excavation site itself, makes everything easier to understand. According to recent reports, the museum's Butuan branch held learning visits to the excavation site in Libertad in August 2025 and July 2026.

items.title: Half-day course
items.subtitle: The museum plus the balangay site

children.text: Arrive when the museum opens. Start in the Archaeological Hall with the balangay parts and the model.
See the pottery, Chinese ceramics and goldwork, and read the display captions.
In the Ethnological Hall, look at clothing and tools of Caraga indigenous peoples and life in the Agusan Marsh.
Head into the city for lunch.
Take a tricycle or jeepney to the Balangay Shrine in Libertad to see the excavation site and the preserved boat.
Return to the city and stroll the Agusan riverside or the downtown area.
Photography inside the museum is reported to be restricted, so ask the staff at the entrance. Plan the day only after checking the opening days of both the museum and the Balangay Shrine.

items.title: Two days, one night: Butuan introduction
items.subtitle: Museum, sites and city food

children.text: Take your time at the museum on the first morning.
In the afternoon, visit the Balangay Shrine and the excavation site in Libertad.
Try local snacks such as palagsing in the city.
On the second day, continue to other sights in Butuan.
For the second day, see the city guide in the Butuan entry as well.

There are direct flights from Manila to Butuan Airport (Bancasi Airport, BXU). Wikipedia states that Cebu Pacific and Philippine Airlines (operated by PAL Express) serve it, with about 5 to 10 flights a day. Schedules change, so check when you book.
The airport is the only one in Agusan del Norte and the largest in Caraga. The ride from the airport into the city is short.

items.title: From the airport to the museum

children.text: One blogger describes taking the Butuan intra-city multicab (R2) from the airport, getting off near Gaisano Mall and riding a tricycle to the museum. Routes and numbers can change, so check with the driver.
Taxis are reportedly scarce even in the city. Also consider tricycles and app-based rides such as Grab.
Older articles place the museum near City Hall on Jose Rosales Avenue, while maps show it in the Bayanihan district. Confirm the name with a map app and your driver before you set out.
Butuan has long-distance bus terminals, and routes including Manila are reported to operate. Check travel times and fares locally.
Ferry services operate from the nearby Nasipit International Port and the in-city Masao Port. For most travelers, flying is the simplest option.
Tricycles and jeepneys are the basic way to get around. For the Balangay Shrine, you are advised to take a jeepney marked Libertad and then transfer to a tricycle.
Negotiate or ask the fare first when taking a tricycle. Check fares locally.

The museum is an indoor visit, so weather matters little. Butuan does have a tropical rainforest climate, so it is humid and can rain all year. According to the 1991–2020 PAGASA normals cited on Wikipedia, annual rainfall is about 2,125.7 mm, the mean daily maximum is 32.2 degrees and the mean daily minimum is 23.9 degrees.

The wettest month is January (about 326 mm) and the driest is May (about 111 mm). If you plan to walk to the Balangay Shrine or the outdoor excavation site, the period around May is relatively comfortable. May is hot and humid, though, so bring water and a hat.

The city can get crowded during the Balangay Festival centered on the feast of St. Joseph on May 19, the city charter-day events from late July to August 2, and the Kahimunan Festival on the third Sunday of January. Book accommodation early.

Butuan is the central city of the Caraga region, so hotels and guesthouses are concentrated in the city. Prices vary greatly by season and class, so check your dates on a booking site. Half a day is enough for the museum and the Balangay Shrine, so a one-night stay works.

A local snack is palagsing, which Wikipedia describes. It is made mainly in Banza from unaw starch, young coconut and brown sugar, wrapped in banana leaves and boiled for about 30 minutes. Nilubid, a twisted, deep-fried flour snack, is also known as a local specialty. Have your meals in the restaurants of the city center.
Opening days and hours differ between sources, so check the National Museum's official channels or ask locally before you go.
Photography inside the museum is reported to have been restricted. Ask the staff first.
Combining the museum with the Balangay Shrine on the same day connects the story and makes it much easier to understand.
Many captions are in English and Filipino, so a translation app may help.
Older articles and maps disagree on the museum's location, so tell the tricycle driver National Museum and confirm the name.
During the May Balangay Festival, room rates may rise or sell out early.
Saving your map app offline is handy around the heritage sites.
Splitting the day, with the museum in the heat and the outdoor sites in the cooler afternoon, saves energy.
Opening hours, closing days and admission conditions differ between sources. The museum has closed temporarily for repairs before, so always check the latest announcement before you visit.
Older articles place the museum near City Hall while maps show it in the Bayanihan district. Confirm before you set out.
Exhibits may be rearranged or moved to other museums. Famous relics such as the ivory seal or the Golden Tara may not be here.
Some of the Libertad excavation pits are reported to be preserved waterlogged, so bring suitable shoes and an umbrella.
Taxis are reportedly scarce, so plan your return transport in advance.
Observe heritage etiquette and do not touch the artifacts.
